ch14.card: Wrap-up. What is proven, what is not, and what comes next.
ch14.s01.c1: Here is the honest ledger, as of Oct 9. It shows what has a result, and what does not.
ch14.s01.c2: The reader, the thinker and the calculator have results at the smallest size, 3M. That is about three million learned numbers. The thinker works in rounds, and the calculator does exact sums.
ch14.s01.c3: The stop switch, the bell the team rings when done, has never run. The English talker, who writes the answer sheet, is not built.
ch14.s03.c1: Result one. On 6,040 questions kept aside, the model scored 73.01 out of 100 with its thinking on. That is the percent right.
ch14.s03.c2: With thinking switched off, it scored 0.66. A plain model of the same size scored 67.12.
ch14.s03.c3: So the thinking does the work. That is on one copy, at the smallest size. A copy is one separate training run. Bigger sizes are untested.
ch14.s04.c1: Result two. The calculator is plain code outside the model. Think of a pocket calculator. It gets a slip, and sends a reply.
ch14.s04.c2: Over 6 copies, it scored 0.62 points above a similar calculator-inside design. But the likely range includes zero.
ch14.s04.c3: With the calculator switched off, the questions that need it score 0.0. We switch a part off to see if answers break. So the model really uses it.
ch14.s05.c1: The calculator had six pass marks. A pass mark is a bar set before the run. Four passed. Two were not clean.
ch14.s05.c2: Swap check: with add and sub swapped, answers followed the reply on 5 of 6 copies. The sixth was lost. It checks that the model follows the calculator's reply.
ch14.s05.c3: Wrong-thinking leak check: five of six copies read above the limit of 5. It counts right answers when another question's thinking is swapped in. The project owner cleared it on Oct 9.
ch14.s07.c1: Never run together: the Gemma reader, outside calculator, any-round calls and learned stop.
ch14.s07.c2: The first run is planned at 3M, after the size test finishes. Does bigger help?
ch14.s07.c3: Bigger sizes are unproven. From 3M to 10M, an earlier test gained +0.49 points for ours, and +3.77 for plain. But it had a setting bug.
ch14.s07.c4: The English talker and the race are planned. Games are paused.
ch14.s08.c1: A leak is a right answer with zero thinking rounds. A small leak is a warning light. Six Gemma-reader copies averaged 6.59, against a limit of 4.62.
ch14.s08.c2: Deeper thinking can cost points. The stop may fire too early, which would cut the thinking short, but that is our guess, never shown.
ch14.s08.c3: The big run's web text stays locked until the sealed test questions are fingerprint-checked.
ch14.s10.c1: In order: the size test finishes, then a test of experts, many small specialist networks, not covered here.
ch14.s10.c2: Then a 100M fit check, for memory and speed, and the four pieces together at 3M.
ch14.s10.c3: Then hand-written pieces are replaced. 10M and 30M follow. A results readout is planned for Oct 31.
ch14.s10.c4: One big run waits for clear results, and for the plan to be 90% sure it passes its marks. Marks are bars written down before a run, never moved after.
ch14.s12.c1: The thinking does the work. That is shown on one copy, at the smallest size.
ch14.s12.c2: The calculator can sit outside, like a plain pocket calculator. That is shown on 6 copies at 3M, with two checks not clean. Most of the rest is built or planned.
ch14.s12.c3: The plan's judgment: nothing is ready to buy. It works at 3M, but nobody has shown it improves faster with size than a plain model. Size means more learned numbers.
